name: Maxilla expansion for forward growth (face pulling / reverse-pull headgear)
lead: Reverse-pull headgear, also called a facemask or protraction facemask, is an orthodontic appliance with a frame in front of the face resting on the forehead and chin, with elastics attached to the teeth to pull the upper jaw forward.[7] It is used in children with Class III malocclusion and a retrusive maxilla, often together with rapid palatal expansion.[2]

Orthodontic literature reports that treatment in the deciduous and mixed dentition can produce skeletal forward movement of the maxilla through remodeling of the circummaxillary sutures,[2][4] though it is often accompanied by dentoalveolar effects.[1] Long-term follow-up shows that some patients relapse.[3]
In appearance communities the entry is discussed as a way to move the midface forward, and the evidence concerns growing children, not adults.
infobox: About 14 to 16 hours daily, per Wikipedia[7]

paras: A facemask pulls forward and downward on the upper jaw, the opposite direction of conventional headgear.[7] It is paired with rapid palatal expansion in many protocols, which is thought to loosen the sutures.[2]

The literature has recommended starting before age 8, though one study stated that this had not been supported by scientific data and examined patients younger and older than 8.[2] Another study of 60 Japanese children in mixed dentition examined whether bone age helps plan treatment timing.[4]

A cephalometric study of 41 Class III children found that outcomes were assessed at 5 and, for 18 patients, 10 years after treatment, grouping patients into success or failure; the study explored predictors of long-term failure.[3] A clinical trial in Chinese adolescents examined the effects of maxillary protraction and long-term stability.[5] A Cochrane-style trial cited on Wikipedia suggests early facemask treatment may reduce later need for orthognathic surgery.[7]

Case series with intermaxillary elastics anchored to miniplates in children aged 10 to 13 aimed to achieve skeletal changes with fewer unwanted dentoalveolar effects.[1] Ex-vivo work has studied sutural deformation during bone-anchored protraction.[6]

Clinical studies exist in children with Class III malocclusion: cephalometric follow-ups, a clinical trial in adolescents and small case series.[1][3][5] No studies on adults using facemasks for appearance were found.

card.summary: Orthodontic facemask that pulls a child's upper jaw forward; studied in kids with underbites, not an adult appearance tool.
card.aka: Facemask protraction; reverse-pull headgear; face pulling
card.note: Evidence applies to growing children; some relapse reported.

quick.overview:
Reverse-pull headgear is an orthodontic device used in children with underbites and a recessed upper jaw to pull the maxilla forward.

Studies in children report forward skeletal change, though some patients relapse in the long term.
quick.mechanism: Elastics from the teeth to a frame on the forehead and chin apply forward force, often after rapid palatal expansion, to remodel the sutures around the maxilla.
quick.risks: Dentoalveolar side effects and relapse are reported. Use is guided by an orthodontist, and the evidence concerns growing children.
